Here, we demonstrate a beamstop-free SAXS system comprising layered metallic filters for optimal attenuation of diffraction signals. It enables continuous acquisition of wide q -range/angular scattering signals with a large dynamic range, including the critical small-angle region containing the direct X-ray beam. This method was applied to a two-dimensional array of submicron columnar plasmas generated by irradiating a high-intensity laser pulse onto an assembly of high-aspect-ratio silicon rods with well-defined sharp edges. We experimentally resolve the microscale and macroscale rarefaction dynamics of bulk electrons driven by the pump-laser pre-pulse and main pulse, revealing the initial plasma scale length as a key parameter governing laser absorption in structured targets. Beamstop-free SAXS enables single-shot multiscale structure measurement and establishes a route toward exploration of stochastic plasma dynamics under high-energy-density conditions, including filamentation instability and turbulence.

title: Self-selected motion of overlaid droplets on heterogeneous surfaces via competitive wetting
abstract: Droplets would move following the designed wettability gradient on the surface, toward the position with high surface energy, which is vital for various applications like ink printing, biological detection, and water collection. Anomalously, here we have found that the core of the overlaid droplet shows anti-wettability-gradient movement on the wettability boundary. The core droplet would perform different directional motions after the impact on the same established surface, depending on the impact dynamics and the composition ratio of the overlaid droplet. The macroscopic motion preference of the overlaid droplet is related to the wetting preference of the overlayer on the heterogeneous surface. Competitive wetting/dewetting of different components of the overlayer droplet induces a special shuttle motion of the core droplet. The phenomenon would provide new insight into wetting and droplet control, being promising for broad application scenarios.

title: Pervasive electronic nematicity across the doping-tuned phase diagram of Kagome superconductors
abstract: Kagome superconductors A V 3 Sb 5 ( A = Cs, K, Rb) host intertwined orders arising from electronic correlations and lattice geometry, but the nature of the high-temperature electronic state from which these phases emerge remains poorly understood. Although numerous experiments have reported rotational symmetry breaking, it is still intensely debated whether this may be a simple consequence of the symmetry of the underlying 2 × 2 charge density wave (CDW) or an entirely different mechanism. Here we use spectroscopic imaging scanning tunneling microscopy to track the evolution of electronic structure in CsV 3 Sb 5 as the CDW is intentionally suppressed through two distinct chemical substitution routes—Sn on the Sb site and Ti on the V site. Across a wide doping range, we uncover persistent electronic rotational-symmetry breaking—referred to here as electronic nematicity—forming nanoscale domains with orientations along three crystalline directions. These results demonstrate that electronic nematicity is a persistent feature of the Kagome phase diagram, distinct from the 2 × 2 CDW.

title: Quantitative relationship between coupled structural dynamics and collective order in the original Vicsek model
abstract: While the Vicsek model is widely used to understand active systems, the explicit relationship between structural evolution and the order transition remains an open question. Here we investigate this relationship in the original Vicsek system. We uncover a structure–order relationship across the investigated densities and noise strengths at fixed velocity and particle number, in which the polar order parameter exhibits a general correlation with the average interaction number. Furthermore, we reveal underlying structural self–similarities: cluster–level and system–level interaction number distributions show consistent normalized profiles, alongside a correlation between cluster size and orientation. Building on these correlations, we develop a phenomenological framework that quantitatively relates the order parameter to structural statistics. Moreover, over the investigated range of velocities, the structural features are maintained, whereas the structural–order correlation is augmented by a velocity factor. This work provides a structural perspective on the Vicsek model and suggests a quantitative relationship between microscopic structural organization and macroscopic collective behavior.

title: Multi-scale higher-order contagion dynamics in complex networks
abstract: Real-world social contagions exhibit significant multi-scale features, where behavioral adoption is driven by both microscopic synergistic pressure within tight-knit groups and mesoscopic prevalence across diverse social circles, yet existing studies treat these mechanisms in isolation. Here, we propose a unified multi-scale higher-order contagion model integrating micro-local clustering and meso-structural diversity, and develops a dynamic message passing method to accurately analyze system dynamics. We rigorously derive tricritical points defining the topological boundary between second-order and first-order phase transitions, beyond which significant bistability and hysteresis emerge. While the higher-order effects have a limited impact on the forward threshold, they significantly lower the backward threshold, thereby expanding the active region of propagation. Crucially, structural diversity dually regulates contagion through a competition mechanism between single-component size fragmentation and component quantity gain. This leads to a significant non-monotonic U-shaped variation of the steady-state density with the structural diversity, proving the existence of an optimal structural diversity capable of minimizing the infection scale.

title: Image-based reinforcement learning for robust mode hop recovery in external-cavity diode lasers
abstract: Conventional laser frequency stabilization techniques such as table-lookup or heuristic methods have significant limitations due to intrinsic hysteresis and stochastic mode competition. To overcome this challenge, we introduce a simple hysteresis-aware protocol and a tailored image-based reinforcement learning (RL) framework. This approach enables robust mode hop recovery in external-cavity diode lasers (ECDLs). Using a Rainbow deep Q-network (DQN) trained entirely in simulation, our RL agent achieves 100% recovery success rate across all 163 continuous temperature drifts produced under deliberately extreme perturbations during a three-day stress test. Under challenging discrete test conditions with abrupt current jumps, the success probability reaches 99.9%, with only one failure recorded out of one thousand trials. The controller generalizes well across environmental perturbations, such as temperature fluctuations, without requiring additional calibration. Our approach provides real-time adaptive control with minimal human intervention, marking a step toward fully autonomous operation in quantum experiments and precision optical systems.

title: Modeling non-Poissonian temporal hypergraphs by Markovian node dynamics
abstract: Temporal hypergraphs capture time-resolved group interactions among nodes. Empirical data support that time-stamped group interactions show bursty event sequences and non-trivial temporal correlations. In the present study, we introduce node-driven temporal hypergraph models in which each node stochastically alternates between low- and high-activity states, and a hyperedge produces time-stamped events with a probability that depends on the number of high-state nodes in the hyperedge. For two event-generation rules, we analytically derive interevent time distributions and autocorrelation functions of event sequences, both for hyperedges and nodes. Despite Markovian node-state dynamics, the induced event processes become mixtures of Poissonian, short-tailed components, resulting in longer-tailed interevent time distributions and slowly decaying autocorrelation. The theory further shows the dependence of these features on the size of hyperedge, which largely agrees with various empirical data. We expect our models to provide a simple, interpretable framework for connecting individual-level activity fluctuations to the timing patterns observed in real group interactions.

title: Explaining human cooperation through a dual mechanism of individual and social learning
abstract: Cooperation on social networks is crucial for understanding human survival and development. Human experiments have revealed that individual decision-making substantially influences whether network structure promotes cooperation, but how humans adjust behavior in game interactions remains unclear, especially for payoff-modulated non-imitative adjustments. Here, we formalize such adjustments as experience-based individual learning through trial, payoff feedback, and reflection, and integrate it with imitation-based social learning. We find that individual learning can alter neighbors’ imitation tendencies, and the resulting shifts in the local cooperative environment feed back into the experience-based cognition that guides individual learning. This coupled feedback makes the ability of social networks to promote cooperation largely dependent on whether individuals focus on long-term payoffs, and generates behavioral signatures that help explain previously puzzling and seemingly contradictory cooperation phenomena. Surprisingly, individual learning can outperform social learning in promoting cooperation when its probability is negatively correlated with payoffs. These results help narrow the gap between theoretical predictions and experimental evidence.

title: Perfect supercurrent diode efficiency in chiral nanotube based weak links
abstract: The supercurrent diode effect (SDE) describes superconducting systems where the magnitude of the superconducting-to-normal state switching current differs for positive and negative current bias. Despite the ubiquity of such diode effects in Josephson devices, the fundamental conditions to observe a diode effect in a Josephson junction and achieve perfect diode efficiency remain unclear. In this work, we theoretically analyze the supercurrent diode properties of a chiral nanotube-based weak link. We show a perfect diode effect and anomalous phase can develop across the junction when a magnetic field is applied parallel to the tube despite the absence of spin-orbit interactions in the system. We show the SDE in the junction is independent of the anomalous phase. We determine a persistent current along the nanotube associated with the Little-Parks effect can activate SDE, even in the absence of higher-order pair tunneling processes. We show this type of SDE can lead to, in principle, a perfect diode efficiency, highlighting how persistent currents can be used to engineer high efficiency supercurrent diodes.

title: Efficient adaptive control strategy for multi-parameter quantum metrology in two-dimensional systems
abstract: Quantum metrology leverages nonclassical resources to enhance parameter estimation precision. Hamiltonian control can alter how the parameters are encoded in the quantum state by modulating the quantum dynamics and hence has been developed to increase the estimation precision. However, the optimal control Hamiltonian usually depends on the parameters to be estimated, necessitating adaptive control methods with feedback. Such adaptive control methods have been studied in single-parameter quantum metrology, but not much in multi-parameter quantum metrology yet. In this work, we bridge this gap by proposing an efficient adaptive Hamiltonian control strategy for multi-parameter quantum metrology in two-dimensional systems. By eliminating the trade-offs among optimal measurements, initial states, and control Hamiltonians via a system extension scheme, we derive an explicit relation between the estimator variance and evolution time. Through a reparameterization technique, the optimization of evolution time for each iteration is obtained, and a recursive relation is established to characterize the precision improvement across the iterations. This strategy achieves the optimal performance up to a finite constant multiplicative factor with only a few iterations and is robust against the deviation in the precision of control parameters. Further analysis shows the effectiveness of this strategy for Hamiltonians with arbitrary parameter dependence.

title: Nonlinearity-induced nonreciprocity for evanescent waves
abstract: The reciprocity principle constrains both propagating and evanescent wave regimes, yet magnet-free approaches to nonreciprocal transmission have so far been explored only for waves propagating along the transport direction. Here, we explore and experimentally demonstrate strong nonreciprocal responses for evanescent waves based on tailored asymmetric nonlinearities. By operating in the bandgap of a coupled-resonator system and exploiting engineered spectral singularities, we show that a saturable nonlinear defect enables pronounced nonreciprocal transmission under evanescent-wave excitation. Compared with the propagating regime, the evanescent-wave configuration allows a reduced local threshold intensity at the defect, while the required source intensity additionally depends on the evanescent decay between the source and the defect. Our results establish a distinct route to nonreciprocal wave control, extending nonlinear and non-Hermitian scattering physics to waves evanescent along the transport direction.

title: Layer pseudospin superconductivity in twisted MoTe2
abstract: Recent experiments have observed signatures of spin-valley-polarized unconventional superconductivity in twisted bilayer MoTe 2 (tMoTe 2 ). Here, we explore the rich physics of superconducting tMoTe 2 , enabled by its unique layer-pseudospin structure. Within a minimal two-band model, both interlayer and intralayer Cooper pairings can be effectively visualized on a layer-space Bloch sphere. Importantly, we find that interlayer pairing dominates in the spin-valley-polarized state, while intralayer pairing prevails in the spin-valley-unpolarized state. We further predict that, for the spin-valley-polarized intravalley superconducting state, experimentally feasible weak displacement fields can stabilize finite-momentum pairing at low temperatures. Additionally, in-plane magnetic fields, which break three-fold rotational symmetry, induce field-direction-dependent finite-momentum pairing states, yielding a versatile momentum-selection diagram. Our work highlights the pivotal role of layer pseudospin in tMoTe 2 ’s unconventional superconductivity and demonstrates its unique tunability via external fields.

title: Dynamical superfluid and Bose-insulator phases in quantized microcavity lattices
abstract: Microcavity exciton-polaritons have emerged as an excellent platform for realizing quantum phases of matter, owing to their ability to undergo non-equilibrium Bose-Einstein condensation. Here, we show that the interplay between multiple quantized levels in microcavities and polariton nonlinearity drives the emergence of unconventional phases. Specifically, we demonstrate that intra-site quantization in microcavity polariton lattices—manifested as multiple energy levels in strongly confined sites—provides a route to manipulating these phases. We show that nonlinear interactions transfer population into excited onsite energy levels, acting as an intrinsic dynamical channel that controls coherence across the lattice. While weak nonlinearity confines polaritons to the lowest mode, yielding a robust superfluid phase with broken U (1) symmetry, strong nonlinearity induces phase diffusion through inter-level mixing. This dynamically generated fluctuation suppresses global phase coherence and drives the system into a dynamical Bose-insulating phase. Transitions between these phases occur either as a non-equilibrium phase transition or a sharp crossover.

title: Time-reversal symmetry breaking and inherent Josephson diodes in a multi-component order parameter superconductor
abstract: Spontaneous time-reversal symmetry breaking is a defining feature of unconventional superconductivity and a prerequisite of the technologically relevant superconducting diode effect. However, its realization remains rare and exclusive to proximity-engineered weak links. Here we examine an alternative pathway to spontaneous time-reversal symmetry breaking by studying junctions that appear in single-crystal microstructures of the unconventional superconductor Sr 2 RuO 4 , lacking external superconducting proximity. We interpret the Josephson coupling as superconducting domains of a multi-component order parameter based on a plethora of anomalous effects — including a field-free Josephson diode effect, fractional Shapiro steps, magnetic interference patterns deviating from the conventional flux quantum periodicity, and bias current-programmable bistable states. These microscopic devices corroborate earlier bulk probes of time-reversal symmetry breaking, giving a renewed impulse to the long-debated pairing symmetry of Sr 2 RuO 4 . Our results highlight superconducting domain walls as a platform for functional Josephson devices and the study of fundamental symmetry breaking.

title: Flat Chern bands and correlated states in spiral magnet
abstract: Flat topological bands provide a promising platform for realizing exotic correlated quantum phases such as fractional Chern insulators. Here, we predict the van der Waals monolayer ReAg 2 Cl 6 hosts isolated flat Chern bands at the Fermi level in its 120 ∘ antiferromagnetic ground state. Their flatness and nontrivial topology arise from the interplay between coplanar spin order and strong spin-orbit coupling within Re 5 d orbitals, providing a mechanism distinct from moiré systems. The spiral spin texture naturally enlarges the unit cell, reducing carrier densities while preserving sizable interaction scales. Many-body calculations show that fractional fillings of the flat bands can stabilize correlated phases, including fractional Chern insulators and charge-density-wave states. Moreover, the mechanism is generic to a broad family of Re-based compounds, with both spin configuration and flat band topology electrically tunable. These findings establish Re-based coplanar antiferromagnets as a robust, tunable, and experimentally accessible platform for flat Chern bands and correlated topological phases potentially at elevated temperatures.

title: Anisotropic light-electron-phonon coupling and ultrafast carrier separation in ferroelectric BaTiO3
abstract: Ferroelectric materials with built-in electric fields are useful for ultrafast electronics and conversion of light into electrical energy, yet the interaction of carrier motion with ultrafast relaxation processes remains nontrivial. Combining ultrafast electron diffraction with electron microscopy of electromagnetic fields, we capture ultrafast lattice dynamics and nanometer-scale carrier transport in ferroelectric BaTiO 3 . We demonstrated that BaTiO 3 reacts to light with an anisotropic electron-phonon coupling that depends on the optical polarization of the excitation light. Excited electrons relax two times faster into phonons when the optical electric field aligns to the ferroelectric symmetry break. Furthermore, ultrafast electron electrometry captures the motion and separation of photo-excited electron-hole pairs in presence of the ferroelectric field. These combined results provide insight into the tangled and anisotropic interaction of photons with phonons and the ferroelectric field, producing phonons and voltages in a stepwise reaction path.

title: Hierarchical structure of primary and hybridization-induced superconducting correlations in bilayer nickelates
abstract: The discovery of high-pressure superconductivity in the bilayer nickelate La 3 Ni 2 O 7 , with a transition temperature approaching 80 K, has stimulated intense debate regarding its microscopic origin. Although an s ± gap symmetry has been widely proposed, the electronic degrees of freedom responsible for pairing remain unsettled. Here we investigate a bilayer two-orbital Hubbard model using the variational Monte Carlo method and reveal a hierarchical pairing structure in bilayer nickelates. The primary pairing tendency originates from the bonding–antibonding splitting of the Ni \(3{d}_{{z}^{2}}\) orbitals, while orbital hybridization redistributes superconducting correlations to the \({d}_{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}\) channel despite its weak intrinsic pairing tendency. This distinction between the origin of pairing and the resulting superconducting correlations explains why the two orbital channels exhibit comparable long-range correlations. The resulting s ± state is robust against changes in Fermi-surface topology. These results reconcile apparently competing theoretical scenarios and provide a comprehensive understanding, highlighting the distinctive role of orbital hybridization in multilayer correlated superconductors.

title: Acoustically controlled polarization states of resonant γ-photons
abstract: Coherent control of light and its interactions with matter is a key aspect of quantum optics. Nuclear resonant interactions enable coherent manipulation of photons at X-ray and γ -ray energies. One promising approach to manipulating γ -photons emitted by radioactive sources exploits ultrasonically vibrating nuclear resonant absorbers. However, previous studies have focused on unpolarized γ -radiation interacting with isotropic resonant media without exploiting polarization effects. Here, we demonstrate simultaneous temporal control of the waveform and polarization state of γ -photons by combining ultrasonic vibrations of magnetically ordered resonant absorbers with anisotropy in nuclear resonant scattering. This method allows interlinking phase differences of individual resonant interaction paths with their polarization dependence. A particular consequence is the possibility to form double-pulse γ -radiation sequences with tunable time-dependent polarization states. Using the reported method, coherent control of γ -photons can be expanded to polarization-based experiments and related applications in quantum optics can be further explored using a tabletop γ -optical setup.

title: On-demand instantaneous bandwidth microwave receiver via scalable Rydberg Vapor cell array with Stark comb
abstract: Rydberg-atom-based microwave (MW) sensors offer high sensitivity and intrinsic traceability, but their instantaneous bandwidth is fundamentally limited by atomic coherence time. Here, we introduce a scalable sensing architecture that overcomes this limitation by spatially multiplexing atomic detection channels with a Stark comb, in which an MW frequency comb (MFC) and a position-dependent Stark field enable each Rydberg vapor cell to function as an independent frequency-selective heterodyne receiver. We experimentally validate the 210 MHz instantaneous-bandwidth channelized receiver architecture through sequential characterization of individual Stark-shifted channels using a 21-line MFC, while maintaining an overall sensitivity of 326.6 nVcm −1 Hz −1/2 despite a 160 MHz tuning of the carrier resonance frequency. Full simultaneous operation across the 210 MHz bandwidth requires parallel implementation and readout of all channels. This scalable architecture enables on-demand instantaneous bandwidth while preserving sensitivity, providing a pathway toward real-time broadband MW detection for radar, communications, and spectrum monitoring.
keywords: Atomic and molecular interactions with photons

title: Synthetic 2D quantum materials from atomic weaving of 1D nanoribbons
abstract: The bottom-up van der Waals (vdW) assembly of quantum materials from low-dimensional building blocks provides a flexible and structurally defined route for designing materials with tailored quantum properties. While stacking two-dimensional (2D) vdW materials has yielded highly tunable platforms for emergent topological and correlated phenomena and has opened pathways toward three-dimensional (3D) layered architectures with extensive lateral design flexibility, the bottom-up vdW assembly of other low-dimensional materials remains largely unexplored. Here, we propose an atomic-scale Lego construction strategy that assembles 2D materials from 1D nanoribbons, embedding design freedom at the structural level through atomic-scale control over lattice geometry, stacking, and edge configuration. Using graphene nanoribbons (GNRs) as a prototype, we develop a general weaving approach that interlaces flat or curved ribbons into stable, periodic 2D networks-analogous to stacking 2D sheets into 3D crystals, but instead progressing from 1D elements to 2D architectures. The resulting woven GNRs (w-GNRs) exhibit geometry-dependent electronic behavior: ribbon width determines the band gap, while inter-ribbon spacing controls the bandwidth and leads to flat-band formation near the Fermi level. By weaving curved ribbons, we construct kagome and square lattice configurations that host symmetry-protected flat bands and orbital degeneracies. This atomic Lego framework enables scalable construction of artificial 2D materials from 1D components, expanding the design space for highly tunable 2D systems with emergent quantum properties.

title: Real-time dual-telescope normalization for improved density estimation in absorption muography
abstract: Absorption muography infers path-averaged density from the attenuation of atmospheric muons. Transient flux variations driven by weather, solar activity, and geomagnetism bias sequential measurements that rely on a non-simultaneous background. Here we show a real-time dual-telescope normalization in which two identical plastic-scintillator telescopes operate in parallel, one viewing open sky as a reference and one viewing the target. Their count-rate ratio cancels common-mode flux changes and tracks detector drift. A 140-h no-target run yields a stable calibration, and stacked acrylic slabs give an empirical transmission–thickness curve. Applied to blind targets, the dual-telescope workflow recovers the densities of 20-cm aluminum and 10-cm stainless-steel blocks within uncertainties, whereas a single-telescope workflow shows systematic biases of +18.95% and −22.82%. A vertical stack of the two telescopes further improves common-mode rejection, reducing calibration ratio scatter from 7.6% to 3.3%. The method is model-independent, removes systematic density biases in any campaign where a simultaneous flux reference is feasible, and is directly applicable to field deployments.

title: Performance analysis of classical adiabatic annealing on Ising machines
abstract: Ising machines are a promising approach to solve optimization problems. They map them onto the Ising model and search for low-energy configurations. However, navigating the rugged energy landscapes remains difficult. To improve this navigation, classical adiabatic annealing has been proposed as a heuristic optimization method for classical Ising machines. Using this technique, the Hamiltonian of the Ising machine is gradually transformed from an easily solvable Hamiltonian to the target Hamiltonian. However, its claimed effectiveness is primarily motivated by an analogy to quantum adiabatic annealing, and systematic benchmarking has remained limited. In this work, we investigate the potential of classical adiabatic annealing as an optimization strategy for analog Ising machines. Using continuation methods, we analyze its dynamics and identify saddle node bifurcations as a key mechanism limiting performance. Motivated by this insight, we develop an optimized annealing strategy we refer to as hybrid classical adiabatic annealing, designed to circumvent these bifurcations and assess its performance. Although the proposed approach can improve convergence to optimal solutions, numerical simulations show only marginal performance gains compared to other optimization strategies. We therefore conclude that, while the hybrid strategy can offer occasional benefits, it does not provide a sufficient practical advantage over simpler, existing techniques.
keywords: Statistical physics, thermodynamics and nonlinear dynamics

title: Suppression of stripe-ordered structural phases in monolayer IrTe2 by a gold substrate
abstract: Metal-assisted exfoliation of two-dimensional (2D) materials has emerged as an efficient route to isolating large-area monolayer crystals, yet the influence of the supporting metal substrate on their intrinsic properties remains poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate successful gold-assisted exfoliation of monolayer IrTe 2 up to the millimeter scale. Angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES), combined with first-principles calculations, reveals that the low-energy electronic structure closely resembles that of a freestanding monolayer 1T-IrTe 2 . We find that quasi-covalent hybridization together with substrate-induced strain leads to only modest modifications of the electronic bands. Although strain contributes to phase stability, it is essentially hybridization that drives the stabilization of the 1T-phase of the monolayer IrTe 2 by suppressing stripe-ordered phase transitions. These results establish gold-assisted exfoliation as a robust route to prepare a large-area monolayer IrTe 2 and highlight the role of metal-substrate interaction in engineering 2D materials with tailored structural phases.

title: Twisted shock waves enable ballistic microparticle manipulation
abstract: The ability to control the motion of microscopic objects in liquids is important for applications ranging from microfluidics to the study of fast hydrodynamic processes. However, conventional optical and acoustic manipulation techniques rely mainly on continuous forcing, limiting access to impulsive dynamics on nanosecond timescales. Here we show that spiral-shaped nanosecond laser pulses focused into a thin liquid layer generate twisted shock waves with tunable angular momentum and peak pressures on the order of gigapascals. Time-resolved shadowgraphy and two-dimensional hydrodynamic simulations independently show the same dependence on the spiral geometry, revealing that the angular momentum can be controlled through the excitation shape. We further show that a 10- μ m polystyrene particle exhibits loop-like ballistic motion on nanosecond timescales, with complementary measurements along two orthogonal directions supporting this interpretation. These results provide an impulse-driven approach for controlling and probing ultrafast particle dynamics in liquids, with potential applications in high-pressure microfluidics, microrheology, and short-time hydrodynamics.

title: Photoluminescence from Cr3+ excited orbital states in magnetically ordered CrCl3
abstract: Control of magnetic order through optical manipulation of orbital states can be realized in a wide range of materials, including insulators. In the latter case, electrons are excited into different electronic states, whose character may be a complex result of spin-orbit-lattice coupling. Here, we use a combination of polarization-resolved photoluminescence spectroscopy and density functional theory calculations to study excited Cr 3+ ions in bulk, insulating, antiferromagnetic CrCl 3 . Our results demonstrate a temperature-dependent preferential polarization direction below ~17 K, which reorients in the presence of an applied in-plane magnetic field. Density functional theory calculations reveal a local distortion of the ligand field and the generation of out-of-plane spin and orbital moments, following the excitation of Cr 3+ ion. These changes link the photoluminescence polarization to the magnetic state of CrCl 3 . Our findings provide insight into the electronic structure of excited-state Cr 3+ ions and suggest that CrCl 3 is a promising candidate for opto-orbitronic applications.

title: Sub-wavelength mid-infrared imaging of locally driven photocurrents using diamond campanile probes
abstract: Precise and high efficiency concentration of mid-infrared (mid-IR) light into sub-wavelength volumes is essential for probing low-energy excitations and achieving strong field enhancements, which is hindered by absorption losses and coupling inefficiencies at long wavelengths. Here, we introduce a diamond-based metal-insulator-metal campanile probe that adiabatically compresses free-space mid-infrared light (10 μm) into ≈ 0.7 μm domain. Integrated into a scanning photovoltage microscope, the probe enables sub-wavelength mapping of locally driven photocurrents in graphene, resolving polarization-dependent and contact-sensitive responses at energies down to ≈ 0.1 eV. Experiments reveal a photocurrent signal density enhancement of 10 3 , coupling light power efficiencies above 1%, and an 18-fold increase in near-field light flux density, in agreement with numerical simulations. Operation of the probe with quantum cascade and free-electron lasers demonstrates a robust, spectrally tunable platform for high-resolution exploration of low-energy carrier dynamics in atomically thin materials, opening opportunities for mid-IR optoelectronics and quantum photonics.

title: Electrical conductivity structure drives anomalous and potentially time-varying magnetic fields at Uranus and Neptune
abstract: Uranus and Neptune exhibit magnetic fields that are non-dipolar and non-axisymmetric, unlike those of any other known planet. These fields are generated by fluid motions in electrically conducting planetary interiors via dynamo action, offering a window into otherwise inaccessible deep processes. Understanding why Uranus and Neptune have such unusual magnetic fields provides critical insight into dynamo processes across planets and stars. Here, we present numerical dynamo models that produce large-scale magnetic features consistent with the observed fields of Uranus and Neptune, with the radial profile of electrical conductivity — controlled by interior composition and temperature — being a critical ingredient. These non-dipolar dynamos exhibit substantial temporal variation, although the rate fluctuates and can be transiently slow. Changes in the intensity and/or orientation of Uranus’ and Neptune’s magnetic fields are therefore plausible over more than 30 years since the Voyager 2 flybys, though the extent of any such variation remains poorly constrained observationally as each planet has been measured in situ only once. This potential secular variation can affect the interpretation of auroral observations and inform planning for future missions to the Uranian and Neptunian systems.

title: Single-file diffusion of charged particles on a devil’s staircase
abstract: Controlling how particles diffuse through low-dimensional materials, where long-range repulsion couples every particle to every other, is central to ionic conductors, intercalation compounds, and many confined transport systems. Yet how such repulsion shapes diffusion at realistic temperatures has remained poorly understood, because the ordered states it stabilizes and the rare hops that govern motion are difficult to treat analytically or to sample numerically. Here we show, by combining large-scale simulations with a theoretical framework, that diffusion is sharply suppressed at a hierarchy of commensurate densities forming a devil’s staircase, most prominently at one-half, one-third, and two-thirds filling, and that random defects destabilize these ordered states and restore transport. To explain this, we represent particle configurations as evenly spaced building blocks whose rearrangements map the complex interacting system onto a simple symmetric exclusion process. Our results provide a unified, quantitative account of diffusion suppression in long-range interacting materials.

title: Phase-binarized auto-oscillation modes in wide nanoconstriction spin Hall nano-oscillators
abstract: Nanoconstriction spin Hall nano-oscillators (SHNOs) are cutting-edge spintronic devices for gigahertz signal generation and neuromorphic computing, offering a CMOS-compatible nanoscale footprint, ultra-wide frequency tunability, and robust synchronization in large networks. Most previous studies have focused on constrictions narrower than 200 nm, where a single dominant spin-wave mode typically emerges. The auto-oscillation dynamics of wide constrictions remain largely unexplored. Here, using micromagnetic simulations, we demonstrate the coexistence of two independently tunable auto-oscillation modes in constrictions wider than 200 nm: a low-frequency in-phase mode and a high-frequency out-of-phase mode, both localized at opposite constriction edges. The out-of-phase mode arises from the interplay of exchange, magnetodipolar coupling, and the antisymmetric Oersted field component, producing strongly edge-localized oscillations with a nearly 180 ∘ phase difference. We develop an analytical two-mode framework that captures their hybridization and nonlinear competition. Their distinct subharmonic injection-locking responses enable phase-binarized states within a single wide SHNO, opening opportunities for multimode synchronization, unconventional computing, and complex phase locking in SHNO networks.
